docs.title: The Sum Function in C++
docs.text:
Author(s):

(RGB) Raghav B. Venkataramaiyer <bv.raghav -at- thapar -dot- edu>

This project creates a sum function in c++ as a sample to illustrate how to compile a shared library and distribute it for use along with the binary.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
make -C code

This will create create a folder dist in code folder, with following contents

dist
 +-lib
 |  \-libbvr_math.so
 +-bin
    \-run

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cd code
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=dist/lib
./dist/bin/run

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Week 1 : Order of Flags in Compilation Command
Error:
docs.text:
Error encountered during compilation.

run_main.cpp:(.text.startup.main+0x68): undefined reference to `Bvr::Math::sum(int, int)'

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
In my Makefile, I define the recipe for binary file as,

dist/bin/run : src/bin/run_main.cpp 
    $(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(CFLAGS) $(LDFLAGS) $(FLAGS) \
           -lbvr_math -o $@ $^

which during make translates to,

c++ -O2 -Wall -Wextra -fPIC -std=c++17 -Iinc \
    [...]                                    \
    -Ldist/lib -lbvr_math -o dist/bin/run    \
    src/bin/run_main.cpp

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: In this case the most likely error is in the order that -lbvr_math precedes src/bin/run_main.cpp. Whereas, -lbvr_math, should follow src/bin/run_main.cpp.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
In the Makefile, the recipe should instead be defined as:

dist/bin/run : src/bin/run_main.cpp 
    $(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(CFLAGS) $(LDFLAGS) $(FLAGS) \
           -o $@ $^ -lbvr_math

Because

The generic definition of a recipe in Makefile is:

output_filename : dependency1 dependency2 [...]
    shell_command -o $@ $^

Assuming that the shell_command accepts a flag -o for output filename and a list of input filenames to process.

docs.title: Work Completed
docs.text:
• Prepared the ThreatLens Prototype Stage Report for MST evaluation, covering the problem statement, architecture, implementation, testing, results and future scope.
  • Tested the end-to-end scan on the controlled test-repo and reviewed findings from Gitleaks, OSV-Scanner and Semgrep.
  • Debugged scanner exit-code handling: exit code 1 can mean findings were detected, so it should not automatically be treated as a crash.
  • Reviewed the report output and worked on making the “How to fix” guidance more useful, especially for vulnerable dependencies: check the patched version, upgrade the package, update requirements.txt/lock files, and re-run the scan.
  • Reviewed the CLI reporting options: HTML report by default, terminal text using --text, and machine-readable JSON using --json.
  • Reviewed JSON output intended for future VS Code integration. It includes a schema_version, relative file paths, severity, message, risk, fix, reference and scanner status.
  • Reviewed GitHub scan workflow support in the current code, including repository/branch selection, scanning and report generation.

docs.title: Commands for Testing / Demonstration
docs.text:
Run a local scan and generate an HTML report:

python threatlens.py test-repo

Print the full text report in the terminal:

python threatlens.py test-repo --text

Print machine-readable JSON:

python threatlens.py test-repo --json

Write the HTML report without automatically opening the browser:

python threatlens.py test-repo --no-open

Scan a GitHub repository (requires valid GitHub authentication configured for the project):

python threatlens.py --github OWNER/REPO

List branches for a GitHub repository:

python threatlens.py branches OWNER/REPO

docs.title: Difficulties and How They Were Addressed
docs.text:
• Different scanner output formats: Each scanner's output is converted into the shared Finding structure before reporting.
  • Exit code 1 when findings exist: Scanner wrappers distinguish “issues detected” from an actual execution failure.
  • Fix guidance was too general: Reviewed the recommendations and made the dependency-fix steps more actionable. OSV recommendations direct the developer to check patched versions, update dependencies and scan again. Semgrep recommendations still include general guidance and references, so they can be improved further.
  • Reports need to support both people and programs: HTML and text output help developers, while JSON output uses a stable schema for future integration.
  • Incomplete scans must be visible: The report shows scanner failures instead of silently implying that all scanners completed successfully.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The prototype report was prepared for MST evaluation. Testing and debugging focused on the scan/report flow and making the “How to fix” section clearer. The controlled test-repo produced 36 findings in the documented run; this is a result for that test repository, not a claim about all possible vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Next Improvement
docs.text: Make Semgrep recommendations more rule-specific, add automated tests for report generation and failure cases, and continue validating that sensitive values never appear in generated reports.

docs.title: Week 1: Problem Identification, Planning and Initial Research
1. Problem Identification
docs.text:
The idea for this problem actually came from something we noticed firsthand. One of our friends had built and deployed a website, and while casually going through it, we opened the browser inspector out of curiosity. We found that some API tokens were exposed right there in the network requests, and using them, it was possible to access other users' data on that platform. This wasn't something we were even looking for; it just turned up during normal use of the site.

That one incident got us thinking about how common this kind of issue might actually be, especially now that a lot of code is being written with the help of AI tools. AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but the generated code may sometimes contain security issues such as hardcoded passwords or API keys, unsafe coding practices, vulnerable dependencies, or improper access control.

We also noticed that there are already different tools available for finding different types of security problems. For example, one tool may detect leaked secrets while another checks dependencies or insecure code patterns. Using different tools separately can make the development process confusing and can also make security issues difficult to track.

Another issue we identified was that security problems are sometimes detected late, after the code has already been pushed, merged, or deployed — much like how our friend's issue was only noticed by chance, after the site was already live.

Based on these observations, we decided to work on an AI-Code Security Platform that can help identify security issues in AI-generated code at different stages of the development process.

docs.title: 2. Idea Selection
docs.text:
After discussing the problem, we finalized the idea of building an AI-Code Security Platform--ThreatLens .

The main idea is to have security checks at different points in the development workflow instead of checking the code only after it has been completed.

The initial workflow we discussed was: AI Prompt -> AI Generated Code -> IDE / Editor -> GitHub Repository -> Scheduled Deep Scan

To make the workflow more visible and to keep track of the project easily, we divided it into four main modules as follows:

  1. Module 1 – GitHub Repository Scan
  2. Module 2 – IDE / Editor Check
  3. Module 3 – AI Prompt Hardening
  4. Module 4 – Scheduled Deep Scan

The main idea was that to have a common security engine will be used so that the security rules and the format of the findings can be reused by different modules.

docs.title: 3. Team Discussion and Brainstorming
docs.text:
A meeting was conducted with the team members to discuss the possible functionalities of the project.

During the meeting, we first listed as many possible features as we could think of and then discussed which features were actually useful and feasible to implement.

The main functionalities discussed were:

docs.title: Module 1 – GitHub Repository Scan
docs.text:
• Connect the platform with a GitHub repository
  • Scan the repository for security issues
  • Detect hardcoded passwords, API keys and other secrets
  • Check for outdated or vulnerable dependencies
  • Detect common unsafe coding patterns
  • Generate a security report
  • Explain the detected issue in simple language
  • Suggest a possible fix
  • Post the result directly on the Pull Request

docs.title: Module 2 – IDE / Editor Check
docs.text:
• Check newly written or pasted code
  • Detect security issues while the developer is coding
  • Show warnings inside the editor
  • Prevent new security issues from being pushed to GitHub

docs.title: Module 3 – Prompt Hardening
docs.text:
• Check the AI coding prompt before the code is generated
  • Add security related instructions to the prompt
  • Encourage secure coding practices
  • Include instructions such as using environment variables and parameterized queries

docs.title: Module 4 – Scheduled Deep Scan
docs.text:
• Run deeper security scans periodically
  • Find issues that may require more time to analyze
  • Identify unused or unnecessary files
  • Identify outdated documentation
  • Generate a combined report and dashboard

docs.title: 4. Selecting the Functionalities
docs.text:
After brainstorming, we discussed which functionalities should be included in the project and which ones could be kept for later stages.

One of the main decisions was that the project should not try to implement every feature at the same time.

The four modules were kept as the overall project structure, but the implementation would be done one module at a time.

we decided to start with module one .The first version was therefore planned around this sequence:

Repository -> Security Scan -> Find Security Issues -> Generate Report -> Suggest Fix -> Show Result on Pull Request

This also gives us a base on which the other modules can later be connected.

docs.title: 5. Deciding the First Module
docs.text:
We decided to start with Module 1 -> Repo Scan and Fix Report.

The main reason for choosing Module 1 was that it covers the basic security scanning functionality and also gives us an opportunity to build the shared security engine early.

The planned workflow is as follows:

1.GitHub Repository 2.GitHub App / Webhook 3.Security Engine 4.Security Scanners 5.Findings 6.Finding Normalization 7.Deduplication 8.Risk Ranking 9.Plain Language Explanation 10.Fix Recommendation 11.GitHub Pull Request Comment

The first implementation will start with a smaller version of this workflow, and additional scanners/features will be added gradually.

docs.title: 6. Research on Existing Open-Source Tools
docs.text:
After deciding to start with Module 1, we researched existing open-source tools that could be integrated into our project.

The purpose was to avoid implementing security detection mechanisms completely from scratch when reliable tools already exist.

The tools considered were: it is represented as requirement--tool considered 1.Secret detection -- Gitleaks / TruffleHog 2.Dependency vulnerability detection -- OSV-Scanner 3.Unsafe code pattern detection -- Semgrep 4.GitHub integration -- GitHub App / Webhooks 5.Scan job handling -- Redis-based queue

The idea is to reuse the existing detection capabilities and focus our own development on how these results are combined, ranked and presented to the developer.

docs.title: 7. Initial Research on Gitleaks
docs.text:
Gitleaks was one of the first tools we started studying.It is useful for detecting possible secrets present in source code or repository history.Some of the types of information we are interested in detecting include:

  • API keys
  • Passwords
  • Access tokens
  • Credentials
  • Other hardcoded secrets

The basic workflow we understood was:

Repository --> Gitleaks --> Scan Files --> Detect Possible Secrets --> Return Finding Information

We also looked at how Gitleaks can provide information about where a possible secret was found.

This is useful for our project because the final report needs to tell the developer which file and line contains the issue.

docs.title: 8. Understanding How Gitleaks Fits Into Our Project
docs.text:
While researching Gitleaks, we realized that Gitleaks itself should not become the complete security platform.

Instead, it should be one component of our Security Engine.

The planned structure is:

Security Engine --> Gitleaks --> Gitleaks Output --> Normalizer --> Common Finding Format --> Explanation + Fix

docs.title: 9. Initial Module 1 Architecture
docs.text:
Based on the discussions and initial research, we designed the first architecture for Module 1.

GitHub Repository
   |
   v
GitHub App / Webhook
   |
   v
Security Engine
   |
   |----> Gitleaks (Secrets)
   |----> OSV (Dependencies)
   |----> Semgrep (Code Patterns)
   |
   v
Finding Normalizer
   |
   v
Deduplication
   |
   v
Risk Ranking
   |
   v
Plain Language Report
   |
   v
Fix Recommendation
   |
   v
GitHub Pull Request Comment

The main purpose of the Security Engine is to act as the common layer between the different scanners and the GitHub interface.

docs.title: 10. Common Finding Format
docs.text:
Another important point identified during the architecture discussion was that different security tools will produce different output formats.

For example:

  1. Gitleaks ~ Secret related result
  2. OSV ~ Dependency related result
  3. Semgrep ~ Code pattern result

If we directly use the output of every tool separately, combining the results later would become difficult.

Therefore, as an initial idea (subject to change once implementation begins), we discussed a possible common format for all findings, with fields such as:

  • ID
  • Tool
  • Type
  • Severity
  • File
  • Line
  • Description
  • Risk
  • Recommendation
  • Status

As a rough illustration of what a finding might eventually look like:

ID: SEC-001 Tool: Gitleaks Type: Secret Severity: HIGH File: app.py Line: 12 Description: Possible hardcoded API key detected. Risk: A credential stored directly in source code may be exposed to anyone who has access to the repository. Recommendation: Move the credential to an environment variable.

This is only a proposed structure at this stage — the actual format may be refined once we start working with real Gitleaks output.

docs.title: 11. Human Approval for Fixes
docs.text:
During the planning stage, we also discussed whether the system should automatically modify the source code when it finds an issue.

We decided that the system should not make changes automatically.

Instead, the system should provide a suggested fix and allow the developer to decide whether it should be applied.

The planned workflow is:

Detect Issue → Explain Issue → Suggest Fix → Developer Reviews → Developer Decides → Fix Applied Manually / With Approval

The same principle will be used for repository cleanup in the later scheduled scan module.

This avoids situations where the system could make an incorrect change to working code.

docs.title: 12. Project Proposal and Presentation
docs.text:
After finalizing the problem, project idea, functionalities and initial architecture, we prepared the project proposal.

The proposal covered:

  • Higher-order goal
  • Time-to-value approach
  • Problem statement
  • Proposed solution
  • Four project modules
  • Engineering approach
  • Detection methods
  • Basic architecture
  • Evaluation criteria
  • Scalability
  • Existing open-source tools
  • Project scope
  • Deliverables
  • Risks and mitigations

The proposal was then presented and discussed.

During this process, the scope of the project became clearer, especially the decision to start implementation with Module 1 rather than trying to develop all four modules together.

docs.title: 13. Outcome of Week 1
docs.text:
By the end of Week 1, the following work was completed:

  • Identified the security problem associated with AI-assisted code generation
  • Finalized the idea of an AI-Code Security Platform
  • Discussed the problem and idea with the team
  • Conducted a brainstorming session for possible functionalities
  • Divided the project into four modules
  • Decided to start development with Module 1
  • Finalized the initial functionality of the GitHub repository scanner
  • Prepared the project proposal
  • Presented and discussed the proposal
  • Researched existing open-source security tools
  • Started studying Gitleaks
  • Identified OSV-Scanner and Semgrep for additional checks
  • Designed the initial architecture of Module 1
  • Planned a common format for findings generated by different scanners
  • Decided that fixes should require developer approval rather than being applied automatically

docs.title: 14. Next Week Plan
docs.text:
The next step is to start the actual implementation of Module 1.

The initial plan for the next week is:

  1. Set up development environment
  2. Install and test Gitleaks
  3. Create a small test repository
  4. Add sample vulnerable code
  5. Run Gitleaks on the repository
  6. Understand the generated output
  7. Create Python wrapper
  8. Convert Gitleaks output into our common finding format
  9. Generate a basic security report

docs.title: Phase 0 – Tool Installation
docs.text:
Installed and verified the security tools required by ThreatLens:

gitleaks version
osv-scanner --version
semgrep --version

These commands confirm that Gitleaks, OSV-Scanner and Semgrep are available from the terminal.

docs.title: Phase 1 – Manual Gitleaks Testing
docs.text:
Created a controlled test-repo containing fake credentials and tested Gitleaks directly:

gitleaks detect --source ./test-repo --report-format json --report-path gitleaks-report.json

This scans the repository and stores the detected secrets in JSON format.

docs.title: Phase 2 – Python Integration
docs.text:
Created:

scanners/gitleaks_scanner.py

Python uses subprocess.run() to execute the Gitleaks command programmatically instead of requiring the user to run it manually.

Conceptually:

subprocess.run([
    "gitleaks",
    "detect",
    "--source", repo_path,
    "--report-format", "json",
    "--report-path", "gitleaks-report.json"
])

docs.title: Phase 3 – Parsing Results
docs.text:
The Python scanner reads:

gitleaks-report.json

and converts the JSON into Python dictionaries/lists for further processing.

The secret value is redacted before the finding is returned.

docs.title: Difficulties Faced
docs.text:
• Gitleaks initially required correct installation/path handling.
  • Gitleaks returns exit code 1 when a secret is detected, which initially looked like an execution failure.

docs.title: How It Was Fixed
docs.text:
• Verified the Gitleaks executable from the terminal.
  • Added handling for the Gitleaks result/exit code.
  • Read and parsed the generated JSON report.
  • Redacted the actual secret before passing the finding forward.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Stage 1 was completed. ThreatLens could now execute Gitleaks from Python and obtain structured, redacted security findings.

docs.title: Phase 4 – Common Finding Model
docs.text:
Created:

engine/finding.py

A common Finding dataclass was introduced so results from Gitleaks, OSV-Scanner and Semgrep could use the same structure.

Important fields include:

tool
rule
category
severity
file
start_line
end_line
description
risk
recommendation
fingerprint

docs.title: Phase 5 – SecurityEngine
docs.text:
Created:

engine/security_engine.py

The SecurityEngine coordinates the scanners and collects their results.

The basic flow is:

SecurityEngine.scan()->Run scanners->Collect findings->Return Finding objects

A scanner failure is handled separately so that one failed scanner does not stop the remaining scanners.

docs.title: Phase 6 – OSV-Scanner
docs.text:
Created:

scanners/osv_scanner.py

OSV-Scanner is executed from Python using a subprocess command similar to:

osv-scanner --format json <repo_path>

The returned vulnerability information is parsed and converted into the common Finding format.

docs.title: Phase 7 – Semgrep
docs.text:
Created:

scanners/semgrep_scanner.py

Semgrep is executed using:

semgrep scan --config auto --json <repo_path>

Its results are parsed and converted into Finding objects.

docs.title: Phase 8 – Normalization and Deduplication
docs.text:
The SecurityEngine combines findings from all three scanners.

The results are then:

Normalize
Remove duplicates
Apply severity
Sort findings

A duplicate is identified using information such as the same file, line and rule.

docs.title: Difficulties Faced
docs.text:
• Gitleaks, OSV-Scanner and Semgrep produce different JSON/output structures.
  • Their findings represent different types of security problems.

docs.title: How It Was Fixed
docs.text:
• Introduced the common Finding model.
  • Created a separate parser/adapter for each scanner.
  • Converted every scanner's output into the same Finding structure.
  • Added normalization, deduplication and sorting in SecurityEngine.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Stage 2 was completed. ThreatLens could run all three scanners and combine their results into one unified collection of security findings.

docs.title: Phase 9 – Severity Classification
docs.text:
Added a configurable severity layer so findings can be classified as:

CRITICAL
HIGH
MEDIUM
LOW
INFO

Example mappings include:

generic-api-key → HIGH
CVSS ≥ 9.0      → CRITICAL

docs.title: Phase 10 – Explanation, Risk and Remediation
docs.text:
Extended each Finding with human-readable information:

description      → What is wrong?
risk             → Why is it dangerous?
recommendation   → How can it be fixed?

This converts raw scanner output into information that a developer can understand.

docs.title: Phase 11 – Security Report Generator
docs.text:
Created:

reporting/report_generator.py

The report generator collects the normalized findings and creates a readable security report.

The complete CLI can be executed with:

python threatlens.py ./test-repo

The command:

python
  |
threatlens.py
  |
SecurityEngine
  |
Gitleaks + OSV-Scanner + Semgrep
  |
Normalize + Deduplicate + Sort
  |
Report Generator
  |
ThreatLens Security Report

A different repository can also be scanned by providing its path:

python threatlens.py "C:\Users\ASUS\Desktop\MyOtherProject"

The report contains information such as:

Repository
Scan time
Finding count
Severity
Tool
Category
File
Line
Description
Risk
Recommendation

Actual secret values are not displayed.

docs.title: Phase 12 – End-to-End Testing
docs.text:
The complete pipeline was tested using the controlled:

test-repo/

The main demonstration command is:

python threatlens.py ./test-repo

The output shows findings from all three scanners in one developer-friendly report.

docs.title: Difficulties Faced
docs.text:
• Raw scanner output was technical and inconsistent.
  • Security findings needed to be understandable to a developer.
  • Actual secrets must never appear in the final report.
  • The project needed a simple way to demonstrate the complete workflow from the terminal.

docs.title: How It Was Fixed
docs.text:
• Added severity classification.
  • Added plain-English descriptions, risks and recommendations.
  • Added secret redaction.
  • Created threatlens.py as a single command-line entry point for the complete scan.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
Stage 3 was completed successfully. ThreatLens now provides a complete local workflow:

Repository
    |
Security Scan
    |
Gitleaks + OSV + Semgrep
    |
Unified Findings
    |
Severity + Explanation
    |
Security Report

docs.title: Yashti’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024030701 Name: Yashti Mittal

  • W4 : Project Setup, Codebase Study and Local Testing
  • W5 : Stage 4 – GitHub Integration, Reports and JSON Output

docs.title: Week 1: Problem Identification, Planning and Work Division
docs.text: Focus: Understanding the problem, choosing the tools, and planning ThreatLens with the team (Rajat, Vidhi, Yashti).

docs.title: 1. Problem Identification
docs.text:
While looking at a friend's deployed website through the browser inspector, we found API tokens exposed in the network requests, and they could be used to access other users' data. This made us look at how often such issues appear, especially now that much code is written with AI tools, which can produce:

  • hardcoded passwords and API keys
  • unsafe code patterns (SQL injection, shell injection)
  • outdated libraries with known vulnerabilities

Different tools already exist for each kind of problem, but developers have to run them separately, the outputs are hard to understand, and issues are often found only after the code is merged or deployed.

docs.title: 2. Idea: ThreatLens
docs.text:
We decided to build ThreatLens, an AI-Code Security Platform with four modules:

  1. Module 1 – GitHub repository scan and fix report
  2. Module 2 – IDE / editor check (VS Code)
  3. Module 3 – AI prompt hardening
  4. Module 4 – scheduled deep scan

Module 1 is the foundation the other modules depend on, so we started there.

docs.title: 3. Choosing the Scanners
docs.text:
Tool Finds Gitleaks leaked secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords) OSV-Scanner libraries/packages with known vulnerabilities (CVEs) Semgrep insecure code patterns

The main problem is that each tool gives its output in a different format, so ThreatLens needs one common format for all findings.

docs.title: 4. The Plan: 5 Stages, 19 Phases
docs.text:
Stage 1 – Local scanning working        Phase 0  Install tools, check versions
                                        Phase 1  Manually test Gitleaks
                                        Phase 2  Run Gitleaks from Python
                                        Phase 3  Python understands Gitleaks output

Stage 2 – Add all 3 scanners            Phase 4  One common Finding model
                                        Phase 5  Security engine
                                        Phase 6  Add OSV-Scanner
                                        Phase 7  Add Semgrep
                                        Phase 8  Normalise / remove duplicates
                                        Phase 9  Decide severity

Stage 3 – Understand + report           Phase 10 Explain the problem
                                        Phase 11 Generate report
                                        Phase 12 Test everything locally

Stage 4 – Connect ThreatLens to GitHub  Phase 13 Connect to GitHub
                                        Phase 14 Select repository
                                        Phase 15 Scan GitHub repository

Stage 5 – Automatic scanning            VS Code extension, findings in the Problems
                                        panel, PR/push scanning and comments

Planned engine flow:

security_engine.py -> run Gitleaks -> run OSV -> run Semgrep
                   -> collect everything -> remove duplicates -> sort by severity

Planned package layout:

engine/      finding.py (common Finding format), security_engine.py
scanners/    one wrapper per tool
reporting/   report generation
github/      Stages 4 and 5
tests/       test code
test-repo/   fake API key, vulnerable dependency, insecure code

docs.title: 5. Work Division
docs.text: Stages Owner Stages 1–3 (local scanning, engine, reports) Vidhi Stage 4 (GitHub integration) Yashti Stage 5 (VS Code extension, PR automation) Rajat

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The team agreed on the problem, the three scanners, the 19-phase plan and the module structure, and each member took ownership of specific stages. My stage is Stage 4: connecting ThreatLens to GitHub.

docs.title: ThreatLens – Week 4 Progress
docs.text: Focus: Project setup, understanding the existing code, and running ThreatLens locally before starting Stage 4.

docs.title: Understanding the Codebase
docs.text:
Before building Stage 4 (GitHub integration), I studied how Stages 1–3 work:

threatlens.py
  |
SecurityEngine            (engine/security_engine.py)
  |
Gitleaks + OSV-Scanner + Semgrep   (scanners/)
  |
Finding objects           (engine/finding.py)
  |
Deduplicate + Sort by severity
  |
Report Generator          (reporting/report_generator.py)

Key points I noted:

  • Every scanner converts its own JSON output into the common Finding dataclass, so the rest of the system never deals with tool-specific formats.
  • SecurityEngine runs each scanner inside try/except, so one failing scanner does not stop the others.
  • Secrets found by Gitleaks are redacted before they reach a Finding.

docs.title: Local Setup (Windows)
docs.text:
Set up the project on my laptop:

python -m venv threatlens
pip install -r requirements.txt
gitleaks version          # 8.30.1
osv-scanner --version     # 2.0.2
semgrep --version         # 1.180.0

docs.title: Rebuilding the Test Repository
docs.text:
The test-repo/ folder in the repository was empty (it had been committed as a nested git repo), so I created a new controlled test repository containing:

config.py          -> fake GitHub token, fake AWS key, hardcoded password
app.py             -> SQL injection, shell injection, pickle, MD5 passwords, debug=True
requirements.txt   -> old flask / requests / jinja2 / pyyaml versions

and ran:

python threatlens.py ./test-repo

All three scanners produced findings, confirming the Stage 1–3 pipeline works on my machine.

docs.title: Difficulties Faced
docs.text:
• Semgrep failed with timed out after 10 seconds on the version check.
  • Running threatlens.py with no folder argument scanned the whole project folder, including my virtual environment: 21 findings, 15 of them false "API keys" inside installed libraries, and Semgrep timed out after 180 seconds.
  • git reported my entire user folder (C:/Users/Yashti) as a git repository.
  • While reading the scanner output, I noticed the same issue being reported more than once (for example, the same token flagged by both Gitleaks and Semgrep).

docs.title: How It Was Fixed
docs.text:
• Semgrep checks the internet for updates every time it starts. Setting SEMGREP_ENABLE_VERSION_CHECK=0 removed the delay.
  • Always pass the folder to scan (python threatlens.py ./test-repo). This also showed that scanning library folders (venv, node_modules) creates noise, which I handled in Stage 4.
  • The user-folder repository came from an old accidental git init and had no commits. I renamed .git to .git_disabled (reversible) so git commands behave correctly.
  • Duplicate findings happen because each finding's fingerprint includes the tool and rule name, so identical issues from different rules are never merged. I recorded this as an open issue for the team.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
ThreatLens runs end to end on my machine, I understand the Finding → SecurityEngine → report flow that Stage 4 builds on, and the Stage 4 work was broken down into steps:

1. GitHub token        5. Clone the repo
2. Connect to GitHub   6. Scan the clone
3. List repositories   7. Always delete the clone
4. Select repo/branch  8. One CLI command + hand-off to Stage 5

docs.title: ThreatLens – Week 5 Progress
docs.text: Focus: Stage 4 (Phases 13–15) – scanning GitHub repositories, plus readable and machine-readable reports. Branch: stage4-github-integration (commit adc6f97)

docs.title: Work Completed
docs.text: All new code is in the github_integration/ package, one file per step.

docs.title: Phase 13 – Connect to GitHub
docs.text:
Created:

github_integration/client.py
  • Logs in with a fine-grained, read-only GitHub token, read from a .env file (git-ignored) or the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable.
  • verify_connection() makes one API call (GET /user), so a wrong or expired token fails immediately with a clear message.
  • All login logic lives in this one file, so changing the login method later only changes this file.
python -m github_integration.client
[OK] Connected to GitHub as yazzzti23
     API calls left this hour: 4999/5000

docs.title: Phase 14 – Select Repository and Branch
docs.text:
Created:

github_integration/repos.py           -> list repositories the token can see
github_integration/repo_selector.py   -> select ONE repository and check it
github_integration/branches.py        -> list branches + branch menu
  • RepoInfo keeps only the fields ThreatLens needs (name, visibility, default branch, size, language, clone URL), so the rest of the code does not depend on PyGithub.
  • parse_full_name() accepts owner/repo, https://github.com/owner/repo(.git), .../tree/main/... and git@github.com:owner/repo.git.
  • select_repo() rejects repositories that are not found or not accessible, are empty, or are larger than 500 MB.
  • Listing branches and asking the user are separate functions. Code with nobody at the keyboard (the VS Code extension, CI) must never wait on input().

docs.title: Phase 15 – Clone, Scan and Clean Up
docs.text:
Created:

github_integration/cloner.py         -> shallow clone into a temporary folder
github_integration/repo_scanner.py   -> remove junk folders, scan, fix paths
github_integration/cleanup.py        -> always delete the clone
github_integration/pipeline.py       -> the whole flow in one function

The flow:

select repo + branch
  |
git clone --depth 1 --single-branch   (token sent as an HTTP header)
  |
remove node_modules / site-packages / caches / virtualenvs
  |
SecurityEngine (Gitleaks + OSV-Scanner + Semgrep)
  |
convert paths to repo-relative ("app/config.py")
  |
delete the clone (always)
  • Token safety: the token is passed to git through environment variables as an Authorization header, never in the URL, so it is not saved in .git/config or shown in the process list, and it is removed from any error message.
  • Exact version: the commit SHA that was scanned is recorded.
  • Always delete: temporary_clone() is a with block. The clone is deleted on success, on an error, and on Ctrl+C. A safety guard refuses to delete anything outside the clone folder, and old leftover clones (>24 h) are removed automatically.
  • Hand-off to Stage 5: scan_github_repo("owner/repo", branch) runs everything, never prompts or prints, and returns the report, branch and commit.

docs.title: CLI and Reports
docs.text:
Updated threatlens.py and created reporting/html_report.py and reporting/json_report.py:

python threatlens.py --github owner/repo                  # branch menu
python threatlens.py --github owner/repo --branch dev     # no menu
python threatlens.py branches owner/repo                  # list branches
python threatlens.py ./folder --json                      # JSON for the extension
  • HTML report: a plain, readable page (summary, findings table, details) that can be saved as a PDF from the browser. All values are HTML-escaped to prevent XSS from content in the scanned repository.
  • JSON output: one JSON object on stdout (relative paths, 1-based lines, null when unknown, versioned with schema_version). Progress messages go to stderr.
  • Exit codes: 0 = no HIGH/CRITICAL, 1 = HIGH/CRITICAL found, 2 = could not run.

docs.title: Difficulties Faced
docs.text:
• ImportError: cannot import name 'Github' from 'github'.
  • Windows could not delete the cloned repositories.
  • Scanning the team repository from GitHub failed with OSV-Scanner exited with unexpected code 128.
  • Gitleaks and OSV reported absolute paths (C:/Users/...), while Semgrep reported relative ones.
  • Raw text output cannot be used by the VS Code extension.

docs.title: How It Was Fixed
docs.text:
• The project's empty github/ folder had the same name as the PyGithub package, so Python imported our folder instead of the library. Renamed it to github_integration/.
  • Git marks files inside .git/objects as read-only and Windows refuses to delete them. remove_tree() now clears the read-only flag and retries.
  • Two problems in scanners/osv_scanner.py: OSV does not search sub-folders by default (our requirements.txt is inside project a/), and exit code 128 means "no dependency files found", not a crash. Added --recursive and treated 128 as zero findings. This bug only appeared on a real repository, not on the local test repo.
  • All paths are converted to repo-relative form once, right after the scan.
  • Added --json and the branches command so the extension can read results with JSON.parse.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
Stage 4 is complete and pushed (15 files, ~1,500 lines). Scanning the team repository from GitHub found 7 MEDIUM issues:

3 x GitHub Actions in .github/workflows/mkdocs.yml pinned to mutable tags (supply-chain risk)
4 x known CVEs in our own requirements.txt (flask 3.0.3, pytest 8.3.2, requests 2.32.3 x2)

Verified: the clone is deleted after success, an error and Ctrl+C; exit code is 1 for the test repo and 0 for the team repo; JSON output parses cleanly.

Open issues: duplicate findings from several Semgrep rules on one line, Semgrep "risk" text showing (A) when OWASP data is a string, OSV findings have no line number, PRs from forks are not handled yet, and tests for github_integration/ are still to be written.
